> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

Researchers sometimes expect people to remain near one of two levels of a psychological outcome, with a rapid transition becoming possible as conditions change.
The stochastic cusp model expresses this possibility mathematically and predicts patterns that can be examined in data.
This tutorial explains the model through diagrams and a synthetic example involving resources, stress, and adaptive functioning.
Readers who know regression and basic R are guided through specifying the model, checking the software's output, and interpreting its predictions.
The example shows how changing stress can produce a predicted distribution with one peak or two, depending also on resources.
It also clarifies why fitting such a distribution to observations from different people cannot by itself show that one person switches between stable states.
We explain which additional observations would help examine that possibility and how to consider competing explanations.
The supplied data, code, and recorded results allow readers to follow the example and adapt the workflow to their own research questions.
When studying psychological change, researchers may encounter gradual adjustments as well as rapid shifts between relatively persistent levels of a response.
Nonlinear dynamical models relate these patterns to the stability of possible responses under changing conditions (Stewart & Peregoy, 1983; van der Maas, 2024).
text.formatted: Nonlinear dynamical models relate these patterns to the stability of possible responses under changing conditions <ref type="bibr">(Stewart & Peregoy, 1983; van der Maas, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The cusp model allows a response to tend toward a single stable level under some conditions and toward either of two under others.
As conditions vary, these levels can shift or lose stability.
A transition may then occur at different points when a controlling factor increases and when it decreases (Grasman et al., 2009).
text.formatted: A transition may then occur at different points when a controlling factor increases and when it decreases <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Grasman et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Even under fixed conditions, a response may fluctuate around a stable level or move between two when both are available.
The stochastic cusp model incorporates these fluctuations and assigns a probability distribution to the response at each combination of predictors.
The predictors can change the shape of that distribution, including whether it has one peak or two (Cobb et al., 1983; Cobb & Watson, 1980; Cobb & Zacks, 1985).
text.formatted: The predictors can change the shape of that distribution, including whether it has one peak or two <ref type="bibr">(Cobb et al., 1983; Cobb & Watson, 1980; Cobb & Zacks, 1985)</ref>.

text.text: Fitting the model allows researchers to estimate these relations and examine the distributions predicted under conditions of interest.
The cusp package makes this approach available in R (R Core Team, 2026).
Its primer introduces the theoretical foundations and demonstrates the software through worked examples (Grasman et al., 2009).
text.formatted: Its primer introduces the theoretical foundations and demonstrates the software through worked examples <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Grasman et al., 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Here, we follow one fixed synthetic example from the model's geometry through its three R formulas to the coefficient estimates and fitted distributions.
We introduce each part of the output when it helps answer a question about the fitted model and show how the available observations constrain the conclusions.
Readers need familiarity with regression and basic R, but no prior knowledge of differential equations.
The accompanying scripts and archived output allow them to follow the analysis (Mabire-Yon et al., 2026); the supplement and companion materials document how the dataset was selected.
text.formatted: The accompanying scripts and archived output allow them to follow the analysis <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(Mabire-Yon et al., 2026)</ref>; the supplement and companion materials document how the dataset was selected.

text.text: Our example concerns how personal resources and acute stress might relate to adaptive functioning.
We suppose that resources favor higher functioning, while stress changes how strongly lower and higher levels separate when both are possible.
These teaching choices guide the model's specification and the interpretation of its predictions.
For this teaching example, we use adaptive functioning to mean how well a person is managing their usual activities and demands at a given time.
We represent it by a hypothetical score, with higher values indicating better functioning.
The person's level of functioning is the quantity whose changes we model: the state variable.
We denote the model's state by 𝑦.
Its connection to the observed functioning score will be specified when we introduce the three formulas.
Figure 1 represents possible state values along the horizontal axis.
text.formatted: Figure <ref type="figure">1</ref> represents possible state values along the horizontal axis.

text.text: A ball's horizontal position indicates the current value of 𝑦.
For now, hold resources and stress fixed.
The shape of the curve specifies which way the state tends to move: in the analogy, the ball moves downhill.
This can mean moving toward a lower or a higher value of 𝑦, depending on which side of a valley the ball occupies.
The curve's height is called the potential.
Its slope determines the direction and rate of change (Grasman et al., 2009; van der Maas, 2024).
text.formatted: Its slope determines the direction and rate of change <ref type="bibr">(Grasman et al., 2009; van der Maas, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: The potential is a mathematical function describing the state's motion, not a measure of psychological energy.
At a valley bottom, the systematic tendency to change is zero: this is an equilibrium.
A small displacement produces a tendency back toward the bottom, making the equilibrium stable.
A landscape with two valleys has two such equilibria.
The hilltop between them is also an equilibrium, but a small displacement produces movement farther away, so it is unstable (Grasman et al., 2009; Stewart & Peregoy, 1983).
text.formatted: The hilltop between them is also an equilibrium, but a small displacement produces movement farther away, so it is unstable <ref type="bibr">(Grasman et al., 2009; Stewart & Peregoy, 1983)</ref>.

text.text: This account sets random disturbances aside: with resources and stress fixed, the slope alone determines how functioning would change from a given starting value.
Section 2 introduces random disturbances.

1.2 Two Controls Shape the Landscape The landscape can change as resources and stress change.
Two parameters called controls, 𝛼 (alpha) and 𝛽 (beta), determine its shape.
The asymmetry control 𝛼 tilts it, favoring higher states as it increases and lower states as it decreases.
The bifurcation control 𝛽 changes the shape around the center.
For suitable values of 𝛼, increasing 𝛽 changes one valley into two.
Such a qualitative change in the available equilibria is a bifurcation; the resulting two-valley configuration is called bistability.
In our example, resources enter 𝛼, favoring higher functioning; stress enters 𝛽, allowing greater separation between low and high states at suitable resource levels.
Both controls determine whether bistability occurs.
Even with positive 𝛽, a sufficiently strong tilt can remove one of the valleys.
The simplest case has 𝛼 = 0: as 𝛽 increases through zero, one stable equilibrium becomes two stable equilibria separated by an unstable one.

text.text: The left side gives the rate of change of state 𝑦.
A positive value on the right indicates a tendency toward higher state values, a negative value a tendency toward lower values, and zero an equilibrium.
For most combinations of the controls, the equation has one or three distinct equilibria.
When there are three, the outer two are stable and the middle one is unstable.
In the landscape picture (Figure 1), the state moves downhill toward a valley bottom.

text.text: Supplement Section S1 gives the potential function that links this picture to Equation 1.
A landscape describes the tendency to change at one fixed combination of 𝛼 and 𝛽.
To see how the equilibria vary across combinations, we collect them in the cusp surface (Figure 2).
text.formatted: To see how the equilibria vary across combinations, we collect them in the cusp surface (Figure <ref type="figure">2</ref>).

text.text: For each pair of controls, retain the state values at which the right side of Equation 1 is zero, and plot them vertically above that pair in the horizontal control plane.
Repeating this across control settings traces the surface.
For a two-valley landscape such as Figure 1B, the values to retain are the horizontal positions of the two valley bottoms and the intervening hilltop.
text.formatted: For a two-valley landscape such as Figure <ref type="figure">1B</ref>, the values to retain are the horizontal positions of the two valley bottoms and the intervening hilltop.

text.text: On the cusp surface, they become three vertically aligned points: the lower and upper stable states, with the unstable state between them.
State 𝑦 has moved from the horizontal axis to the vertical axis; the potential heights of the valleys and hilltop are not plotted.
The surface therefore records equilibrium state values across landscapes, rather than the full shape of any one landscape.
The highlighted section in Figure 2A holds 𝛽 at 1 while 𝛼 varies; panel B shows it face on.

We will use this condition again when reading the fitted control plane.
It applies to 𝛼 and 𝛽, which the predictors determine through the relations introduced below.

text.text: Keep 𝛽 fixed and follow the lower stable branch as 𝛼 slowly increases.
That branch ends at the right fold, so a state following it must move toward the upper branch.
On reversing direction, however, the upper branch persists until the left fold.
The transition points differ according to the direction of change.
This dependence on the history of the controls is hysteresis.
The apparent jump concerns the equilibrium being followed; the state itself changes continuously in time under Equation 1.
Following a branch in this way requires controls to change slowly enough for the state to remain near it, while disturbances are too small to move the state to the other branch first.
A test of hysteresis therefore needs to record the pace and history of the control changes.
The term "catastrophe" refers to a qualitative change such as the loss of an equilibrium.
It can describe improved functioning as well as deterioration; the mathematics does not imply harm.
The cusp surface locates equilibrium states; to describe variation around them, we return to a single landscape.
Hold one person's resources and stress fixed, with their level of adaptive functioning again represented by the ball's horizontal position.

In the stochastic model, the same state variable changes under two influences: the landscape specifies a systematic tendency toward a valley bottom, while random disturbances can move the state in either direction.
These disturbances may also carry it between valleys.
A stable equilibrium therefore describes a tendency to return after a small displacement; it does not require an unchanging state.
Here, randomness represents variation in the state itself.
Estimating measurement error as a distinct source of variation would require an additional measurement model.
With fixed controls, the model can reach a stationary distribution.
This distribution assigns probabilities to ranges of state values, and those probabilities remain constant over time even though the state continues to vary.
The distribution is what cusp() fits (Cobb et al., 1983; Cobb & Watson, 1980; Grasman et al., 2009).

text.text: In our example, it describes possible functioning values at specified resources and stress.
A density curve represents how probability is distributed along a continuous state axis.
The probability of a range of values is the area under the curve over that range; the total area is one.
A peak, or mode, marks a local maximum of density.
In Figure 4, the horizontal axis represents the same state in both rows.

The expression inside the exponential is the negative of the potential.
The factor 𝑍 (𝛼, 𝛽) is the integral of this exponential over the state axis; dividing by it makes the density's total area one.
"Conditional" means that 𝛼 and 𝛽 are held at specified values.

The supplied example uses independent synthetic observations drawn from stationary cusp distributions to illustrate estimation across cases.

Reading such a distribution as the long-run distribution of one person's states additionally assumes that the model describes that person's process and that it has approached stationarity under approximately fixed controls.
Cross-sectional observations alone cannot establish those assumptions or reveal individual transitions.
In the worked example, we hypothesize that resources favor higher functioning and that stress changes how strongly low and high levels separate.
We therefore place resources in the asymmetry control 𝛼 and stress in the bifurcation control 𝛽.
A higher 𝛽 can accentuate both extremes at suitable resource levels, so stress need not act simply by lowering the mean.
The three formulas below express this hypothesis.
The supplied file contains 1,200 synthetic observations and three standardized score columns:
Personal resources (𝑅 𝑧 ): personal_resources_z; higher values represent more re-sources; enters 𝛼.
Acute stress (𝑆 𝑧 ): acute_stress_z; higher values represent more stress; enters 𝛽.
Adaptive functioning (𝑌 𝑧 ): adaptive_functioning_z; higher values represent better functioning; supplies the state mapping.
Each column is centered on its sample mean and divided by its sample standard deviation.
Thus zero represents the sample mean and one represents one sample standard deviation above it.
The score labels do not refer to validated instruments.
Supplement Section S2 provides the generation recipe and exact preprocessing constants; readers use the supplied file directly.

The supplement retains the selection history and all recorded checks.
To fit this model, we need to connect the measurements to each control and to the state axis.
These relations are called mappings; each is written as an R formula.
Here they are linear:
The first two mappings resemble familiar regression equations, except that their predicted quantities are the controls 𝛼 and 𝛽.
The third puts functioning on the model's canonical state axis, the mathematical scale used in Equation 3 with its fixed noise convention.
Although 𝑌 𝑧 already has sample mean zero and standard deviation one, the model still needs to estimate where it belongs on that axis and how widely it extends.
The coefficients 𝑤 0 and 𝑤 𝑌 provide this location and scale.
They are estimated together with the four control coefficients.
For each observation, resources and stress determine 𝛼 𝑖 and 𝛽 𝑖 .
The model then assigns a density to that observation's functioning score, accounting for its transformation onto the canonical axis.
Fitting seeks the six coefficients that maximize the product of these density contributions under independence, or equivalently their summed log likelihood (Cobb et al., 1983; Grasman et al., 2009).

An empirical test would need a credible way to vary or track those resources, with measurements frequent enough to resolve functioning as it changes.
The pace must allow branch tracking, and an ordinary response lag must be considered as an alternative explanation for any loop (van der Maas, 2024).
Reversing stress instead would trace a different path whose predictions need to be specified separately.
Near a fold, the restoring tendency toward a stable equilibrium weakens, and recovery from a small state displacement becomes slower: this is critical slowing (van der Maas, 2024).
To examine it in our example, we would compare recovery at control settings progressively closer to the fold, holding resources and stress approximately fixed during each recovery measurement.
Supplement Section S5 gives the local approximation behind this prediction.
A stressor that increases acute stress would also raise 𝛽 and reshape the landscape.
It would therefore not isolate recovery at fixed controls.
A workable study must distinguish these operations and choose a measurement interval appropriate to the expected recovery time.
The independent observations in our synthetic example cannot test either recovery or hysteresis.

This approach can be useful before a detailed account of the underlying psychological processes is available.

In a phenomenological application, substantive hypotheses guide the choice of state and controls within the proposed cusp form; a mechanistic account instead derives the relevant dynamics from assumptions about those processes (van der Maas, 2024).
The phenomenological model can still yield specific predictions about the conditions under which responses should differ.

These predictions can guide data collection: conditions with two predicted modes invite examination of the conditional distribution, whereas a proposed history-dependent transition calls for observations along a specified path through the controls.
Establishing the processes that generate either pattern requires evidence beyond fitting a distribution.
Whether these predictions can be examined also depends on measurement.

Floors, ceilings, and a small number of ordinal categories can produce patterns that a continuous density represents poorly; standardization does not remove these problems, and transformations require care (Wagenmakers et al., 2005).

The same scientific question should guide the choice of comparison models.
A nonlinear mean function may account for a steep response, predictor-dependent variance for changes in dispersion, and a mixture of populations for conditional bimodality.
Comparisons on the same observations and response scale help assess what the cusp contributes among those alternatives.
They also depend on the conditions sampled: predictions of two modes beyond the observed predictor range remain extrapolations.
Stating the three mappings and their rationale makes clear which relations were proposed in advance and which were explored after inspecting the data.
